120 traces · 2.52B requests

This is a reproduction of a 2023 SOSP paper on cache eviction. The title is deliberately provocative: for thirty years the field has assumed you need LRU plus something clever on top. I re-ran their experiments on two of their datasets, completely, and I will show you where it held up and where it did not.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2302 / 14

Where the eviction algorithm sits

Client
Cacheholds maybe 1% of the data
Backend

Hit

Served from memory, microseconds, backend never touched.

Miss

Full round trip, plus load the backend has to absorb.

miss ratio = misses / requests

The cache is always full, so every admission forces an eviction. Which object gets discarded is the only real lever on that ratio, and at scale one point of it is worth a lot of hardware.

Grounding, keep it short. A cache holds a small slice of the data. A hit is microseconds; a miss is a full round trip plus extra load on the backend you were trying to protect. Because the cache is always full, admitting anything means discarding something, and the rule that picks the victim is the only real control you have over the miss ratio.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2303 / 14

Efficiency bought with complexity

Three decades of work on eviction, and essentially all of it builds on an LRU queue:

ARC · 2Q · SLRU · LIRS
TinyLFU · LeCaR · CACHEUS · LHD

Memory

Two pointers per object, on objects that are often tiny

Throughput

A hit reorders the queue, so it takes a lock on the hot path

Complexity

Parameters that resist tuning, and published LIRS code with two real bugs

So production systems keep running plain FIFO or LRU and absorb the worse miss ratio. The better algorithm never ships.

The setup for the whole paper. Over three decades people built smarter eviction algorithms and essentially all sit on LRU queues. That buys efficiency and costs memory, throughput and simplicity. The authors note that LIRS implementations in prior published work contained two separate bugs. The practical result is the last line: engineers do not deploy these, they run FIFO or LRU and eat the difference.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2304 / 14

The key observation

72%

of objects are requested exactly once within a window holding 10% of a trace's objects

Measured across 6594 production traces. Over a whole trace the figure is 26%, but a cache never sees a whole trace: it sees a window about the size of itself. Most of what you admit is never asked for again.

This is the insight the algorithm falls out of, so spend a moment. People have long measured what fraction of objects are requested only once, and across whole traces it is about a quarter. The authors point out that is the wrong measurement, because a cache never sees the whole trace. Over a window holding ten percent of the objects, 72 percent are one-hit wonders. So most of what you admit is garbage, and the job is to get rid of it fast. They call that quick demotion.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2305 / 14

Ask a cheaper question first

Every LRU variant asks which object is least valuable. S3-FIFO asks whether an object has proved itself at all, which costs two bits.

LRU and its variantsS3-FIFO
Metadata per objectTwo pointersTwo bits
On a cache hitMove to head, take a lockIncrement a counter, no lock
Ordering structureOne or more LRU queuesFIFO queues only
Tunable parametersSeveral, workload-specificOne, and it barely matters

The surprise is the direction. Giving up LRU is supposed to cost efficiency. It buys it.

Frame it as a question rather than a data structure, because that is what is new. Every other algorithm is trying to rank objects by value, which is expensive to maintain. S3-FIFO asks a cheaper question: has this been requested even once since we admitted it? Walk the table. Then the last line, which should be the surprising part: conventional wisdom says FIFO is what you settle for. Here it wins.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2306 / 14

Three FIFO queues

on hitfreq = min(freq + 1, 3)
on insertin G ? M : S
S fullfreq > 1 ? M : G
M fullfreq > 0 ? reinsert, freq-- : evict

That is the entire algorithm. No object is ever moved because it was read, which is why a hit needs no lock.

Walk the diagram left to right, then the code. A new object goes into S, a tenth of the cache. When S fills the tail leaves: promoted to M if it was requested, otherwise dropped with only its key kept in G. If that key turns up again we know it is not a one-hit wonder, so it goes straight to M and skips probation. M evicts like a clock sweep. The four lines are genuinely all of it. Nothing moves on a read, which is where the scalability comes from.

Both datasets I could run are block workloads. The paper's evidence is mostly web and key-value, which are far more skewed. Remember that when the numbers diverge.

Be upfront about scope. The paper runs 6594 traces across fourteen datasets, several terabytes, which a laptop cannot do. I took the two that fit and ran them completely, every trace, not a sample. The algorithms are the authors' own through libCacheSim, so what I wrote is the harness. Land hard on the last line, because it explains every disagreement later: both my datasets are block storage, and block traces are much less skewed than the web traces that dominate the paper. Skew is what this algorithm exploits.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2308 / 14

The paper contradicts itself twice

Section 4.1 says promote when an object was "accessed more than once"; pseudocode line 23 says the counter must exceed one. The prose clears the counter on promotion; the pseudocode never mentions it. So I built all four readings and measured each against the authors' C++.

Promotion ruleReset counterWorst gapDescribed in
freq > 1Yes0.0014Neither alone
freq > 0Yes0.0017The prose
freq > 0No0.0055Neither
freq > 1No0.0058The pseudocode

The match takes its threshold from the pseudocode and its counter reset from the prose. Neither half of the paper is right on its own.

This is what I would lead with if asked what I learned. Two details differ between the prose and the pseudocode, and rather than guess I implemented all four combinations and measured each against the authors' own C++ on the same trace. The highlighted row matches to fourteen ten-thousandths of a miss ratio, and it takes one detail from each half of the paper. Anyone implementing from only the pseudocode, or only the prose, gets a measurably different algorithm.

Result 2 · Miss ratio reduction

First of eleven on the large cache. Paper's mean 14%, ours 14.8%

Original paper

Reproduced ours

The headline. On the large cache size S3-FIFO is first of eleven algorithms and my mean reduction over FIFO is 14.8 percent against the 14 percent stated in their text. Point at the P10 bars too: S3-FIFO stays positive while TinyLFU and LIRS go negative, meaning on the worst tenth of traces those are beaten by plain FIFO. On the small cache my ordering differs, and the next slides explain why.

Original paper

Reproduced ours

Useful because the paper publishes my two datasets as separate rows, so I can check them individually rather than against a pooled average. The win is carried by CloudPhysics: on MSR alone ARC very slightly beats S3-FIFO, 0.132 against 0.131, while on CloudPhysics S3-FIFO is well ahead, 0.151 against 0.110. Result 4 · How big should S be?

The paper's claim is insensitivity, not that 10% is optimal

Original paper

Reproduced ours

I nearly reported this as a disagreement and then realised it is not one. My best setting is 5 percent on the large cache and 25 on the small, not the paper's 10, so at first glance they look wrong. But section 6.2 claims S3-FIFO is not sensitive to the size of S, and their own figure shows a nearly flat mean. They never claim 10 is the argmax. My curve is flat too and 10 is within half a point of the best at both sizes. Check what was claimed before calling something a failed reproduction.
S3-FIFO · Yang et al., SOSP '2313 / 14

Three gaps, one cause

What differsWhy
2Q wins at the small cacheBlock traces are less skewed, so a tiny cache evicts objects before they prove reuse. 2Q reserves fixed space for new objects; S3-FIFO does not.
Smaller absolute gainsSame cause. On the two datasets we share with the paper, its own Figure 7 shows the same narrow margins.
14 MSR traces, not 13The public dataset has 14 files that all clear the paper's 1M cutoff. Request totals still agree: 409.8M against their 410M.

Not a failed reproduction. A reproduction on the two datasets of fourteen that suit the algorithm least.

Had I run the CDN or key-value traces instead, the margins would have been wider and the result less interesting.

Be direct rather than defensive. Every difference traces back to one decision: only two datasets were small enough to run, and both are block storage. The paper's evidence is dominated by web and key-value traces, which are much more skewed, and skew is exactly where quick demotion pays. So I tested the algorithm on its worst ground. If I had picked the CDN traces the numbers would look better and prove less.
